hints: Look at which object each arrow acts on in diagrams A, C and D compared with the Earth and Moon in the other diagram.
Recall Newton's third law needs two bodies, one force on each, of the same type and opposite direction - not just two equal opposite forces on one body.
Check which pair shows Earth pulling one way and Moon pulling back the other way, versus pairs like weight and support both acting on the same resting block.
walkthrough: Identify the bodies: in A both forces act on the car, in C both act on the block, in D both act on the aeroplane, but in the Earth-Moon diagram one force acts on Earth and one acts on Moon.
State the third-law rule: if body X exerts a force on body Y, then body Y exerts an equal, opposite force of the same type on body X.

Test the same-body pairs: driving force versus resistive forces, support force versus weight, and lift versus weight can balance for constant velocity or rest, but they fail the two-bodies same-type test.
Test the Earth-Moon pair: Earth exerts a gravitational force on the Moon, and the Moon exerts a gravitational force back on Earth, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
Therefore only the Earth-Moon gravitational pair satisfies all third-law conditions. This is option B.

options.A: Both the driving force and total resistive forces act on the same car, so they are balanced forces on one body, not an action-reaction pair on two bodies.
options.B: The gravitational force of Earth on Moon and of Moon on Earth are the same type, act on different bodies, and are equal and opposite.
options.C: Weight and support force both act on the same block and are different types of force, so they balance but are not a third-law pair.
options.D: Lift and weight both act on the same aeroplane and arise from different interactions, so they are not a third-law pair.
